query: Which method can be used for concurrent strength–ductility improvement, and why?

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a dual‐phase microstructure consisting of a ductile matrix interspersed with coherent lamellar precipitates (or particles) enables concurrent improvement in strength and ductility in a W-based refractory high-entropy alloy.
generation.material_initial_state: A conventional single-phase or coarse-grained W-based refractory high-entropy alloy lacking engineered microstructural features.
generation.intervention: Tailored processing (e.g., controlled annealing or heat treatment) to form a dual‐phase structure with coherent lamellae (δ-lamellae) and fine precipitates (γ″ particles) within the ductile matrix.
generation.conditions: Tensile deformation at room temperature (and potentially elevated temperatures), where dislocation slip and shearing processes are activated.
generation.structural_mediator: Coherent lamellar precipitates (δ-lamellae) uniformly distributed in a ductile matrix, which interact with dislocations.
generation.mechanism: Under applied stress, dislocations are initially pinned by the coherent lamellae (increasing strength). As strain increases, localized shearing or re-orientation of these lamellae occurs, reducing stress concentration and activating transformation-induced plasticity that improves ductility.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the homogeneous alloy, the treated alloy is expected to exhibit both higher yield strength (due to dislocation pinning) and enhanced ductility (due to controlled lamella shearing and phase transformation) concurrently.
generation.baseline: W-based refractory HEA without the engineered dual-phase (lamellar/precipitate) microstructure.
generation.boundary: The improvement is contingent on achieving and maintaining a coherent, well-distributed lamellar structure; if the precipitates lose coherency or if the phase spacing is not optimal, the concurrent improvement may not occur.
generation.uncertainty: The exact processing parameters needed and the magnitude of simultaneous strength and ductility enhancement remain to be quantified. The interaction of the dual phases under varying temperatures and strain rates also needs further investigation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of W-based refractory HEA samples: one processed under conditions to obtain the dual-phase (coherent lamellar/precipitate) microstructure, and a control group retaining a homogeneous single-phase structure. Perform tensile tests at room temperature while characterizing the microstructure (via TEM/SEM) to confirm the presence or absence of the engineered lamellae.
measurements: Microstructural verification of lamellar coherence and spacing
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the dual-phase processed samples do not show a statistically significant simultaneous increase in both yield strength and ductility relative to the homogeneous control sample, then the hypothesis is considered falsified.

Through TEM observations, we carefully characterized the evolution of the microstructure to discern the salient strengthening mechanisms generated by the SCCPs structure. Dislocation behavior at strains of 4%, 10%, and 14% in the W-based refractory HEA with the SCCPs structure are shown in Fig. 4 . Figure 4a–c, e reveal that dislocations cut through the δ-lamellae, yet are pinned by the γ ″ particles. For the coherent δ-lamellae structure, as the tensile stress increases up to the yield stress, dislocation slip occurs in the fcc matrix and involves shearing across the δ-lamellae, which indicates an early stage of the planar dislocation slip across the coherent δ/γ boundaries (Fig. 4a ). With further increase in strain to 10%, slip bands can clearly be observed across the δ-lamellae (Fig. 4b ). At a strain of 14%, shearing of the δ-lamellae by the slip bands leads to a large local shear (~40%) (Fig. 4c ), rather than the creation of a crack, which alleviates the local stress concentration. A schematic diagram of the interaction of dislocations with δ-lamellae is shown in Fig. 4d .

As such, our alloy design strategy resulted in the discovery of an EHEA with a fine lamellar fcc/B2 structure and balanced high fracture strength and high ductility. This novel strategy is promising to solve the problems inhibiting the engineering application of HEAs as high-temperature materials, including the inferior castability and compositional segregation, and the conflict between high fracture strength and high ductility. In addition, this novel strategy also brought breakthrough to NiAl-based alloys in significantly enhancing the ductility at room temperature while simultaneously achieving the high strength. The EHEA concept, combining the advantages of both HEAs and eutectic alloys, and at the same time eliminating the disadvantages of these two types of alloys, leads to a promising new class of high-temperature alloys. Using this new alloy design strategy, an industrial scale HEA with uniform organizations and compositions can be prepared by the conventional casting method in a low cost way, allowing for large-scale industrial applications.
